short_title: School parcel tax, 48 cents a square foot
official_title: Shall the measure, to strengthen academic excellence, attract and retain teachers, support music/ arts/ athletics/ STEM programs, instructional aides, and for other designated purposes, by imposing a special tax on all real estate parcels, including commercial use, of $0.48/ building square foot, with senior exemptions, independent citizen/ auditor oversight, subject to a tax cap, for 10 years, generating approximately $18,000,000 annually in local funds for Culver City public schools that the state cannot take be adopted?
plain_summary: A new 10-year tax on every property in Culver City, charged at 48 cents for each square foot of buildings on it, up to $15,000 a year per property. The city collects it and gives it to Culver City Unified for teachers, staff, STEM, arts, music, counseling and other programs, not for administrators' pay. Owners 65 or older and people on SSI or SSDI disability benefits don't pay. A committee of residents, parents and school staff would watch how the money is spent.
yes_means: Property owners pay a new yearly school tax of 48 cents per square foot of buildings, up to $15,000 per property, for 10 years, raising about $18 million a year for Culver City Unified.
no_means: No new school parcel tax. Culver City Unified keeps its existing parcel tax of $189 a year per property.
current_law: Culver City Unified already has one parcel tax, a flat $189 a year per property that voters renewed in 2024 (both sides' ballot arguments say so). Measure AA would add to it, not replace it.
fiscal_impact: About $18 million a year for Culver City Unified, per the ballot question. The school district repays the city's cost of collecting it (City Attorney's analysis). LAist reports the tax would start July 1, 2027.
confusing_wording_note: The question calls it a "special tax." A special tax a city council writes needs two-thirds of the vote, but Measure AA started as a voters' petition, so it needs only a majority; the City Attorney's analysis says state law requires approval by "a majority of Culver City voters." Statewide Proposition 43 on this ballot would require two-thirds for future petition taxes starting in January 2027. It's a City of Culver City measure, so only voters inside city limits decide it, even though the money goes to the school district.

supporters_case.text: The parents, residents and teachers who gathered the petition signatures, joined by the presidents of the teachers' and classified staff unions, say Culver City gets "the lowest funding allocation per student possible" from the state, that a committee of parents and residents will plan the spending each year, and that "commercial buildings and movie studios will be asked to pay their fair share" for the first time. Seniors are exempt.

opponents_case.text: John Derevlany says voters approved a $189 school parcel tax and a $358 million school bond in 2024, that this tax would cost about $800 a year for an average-size home, and that it comes during an affordability crisis. He asks voters to "vote for affordability" and vote no.

official_title: Shall an ordinance to maintain Culver City emergency response/ firefighter/ paramedic/ police staffing; affordable housing/ mental health/ homeless reduction programs; improve streets, sidewalks, public transportation, infrastructure, parks and other general fund services by raising Culver City's transient occupancy tax paid by hotel/ motel guests from 14% to 15% until March 1, 2028, and then to 16%, generating up to approximately $2,000,000 annually until ended by voters, requiring annual audits, public spending disclosures, with all funds used locally, be adopted?
plain_summary: Raises the hotel tax that guests pay on stays of 30 days or less in Culver City hotels, motels and short-term rentals, from 14% to 15% on March 1, 2027, and to 16% on March 1, 2028. The money goes into the city's general fund, which pays for city services like police, fire, streets, parks and homelessness programs. It lasts until voters end it.
yes_means: The hotel tax rises from 14% to 15% in March 2027 and to 16% in March 2028, raising up to about $2 million a year for city services.
current_law: Culver City's hotel tax has been 14% since 2012 (City Attorney's analysis).
fiscal_impact: About $1 million in the first year and up to about $2 million a year after that, for the city's general fund (City Attorney's analysis).
confusing_wording_note: The question lists services the money would help pay for, but the tax goes into the general fund, which pays for all city services (City Attorney's analysis). Residents don't pay it unless they stay in a Culver City hotel.

supporters_case.text: Mayor Freddy Puza, Vice Mayor Bryan "Bubba" Fish and Council Member Yasmine-Imani McMorrin say Measure T asks hotel guests, not residents, to help pay for the city services they use, that the rate hasn't changed since 2012, and that 16% matches nearby cities once their tourism fees are counted (Los Angeles 16%, West Hollywood 15.5%).

opponents_case.text: No argument against Measure T was filed with the city.

official_title: Shall the measure amending the City of Culver City Charter to allow Culver City residents aged 16 and 17, who are otherwise eligible to vote under state and local law, to vote on City and School District candidates and ballot measures, provided that each legislative body has approved budgetary funds and determined logistical systems are in place, and that inclusion would not prevent consolidation of City or School District elections with county elections, be adopted?
plain_summary: Changes the city charter so Culver City residents who are 16 or 17 could vote for City Council, on city measures, and for the Culver City Unified school board and its measures. It doesn't start right away. The City Council and the school board must each approve the money, decide the voting systems are ready, and make sure it won't stop them from holding their elections together with the county's. The city clerk told LAist the first chance would be November 2028.
yes_means: 16- and 17-year-olds who live in Culver City could vote in city and school board elections, once the City Council and the school board each decide the conditions are met.
no_means: The voting age for Culver City and school board elections stays at 18.
current_law: You must be 18 to vote in California elections (state Constitution and Elections Code, per the City Attorney's analysis). Culver City voters turned down a similar measure, Measure VY, in 2022; its supporters say it fell 16 votes short.
fiscal_impact: Not estimated. The City Attorney's analysis gives no cost. A city spokesperson told LAist that costs will be estimated after city, school and county staff work out how minors could vote.
confusing_wording_note: A yes vote doesn't let anyone younger than 18 vote right away: the council and the school board each decide, separately, when the conditions are met. It never covers county, state or federal races.

supporters_case.text: Mayor Freddy Puza, Vice Mayor Bryan "Bubba" Fish and Council Member Yasmine-Imani McMorrin say 16- and 17-year-olds already work, pay taxes, drive and volunteer, that city and school decisions shape their lives, and that "people who vote when they first become eligible are more likely to remain engaged throughout their lives."

opponents_case.text: Ron Bassilian of Protect Culver City, Council Members Albert Vera and Dan O'Brien and two former mayors say it "makes our students a captive, impressionable voting bloc," that candidates with access to schools would gain an edge, and that teens would be contacted by campaigns.
